title: Achille Baquet, Barney Bigard and passing for white
summary: On passing in the white union local: Achille Baquet, Barney Bigard's attempt, Bunk Johnson's reaction, and Friganza's 1949 obituary.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: They had a colored local, too?
Out there? Oh, yes, they did out there. They finally went together with the... After a lot of controversy, they finally went together. In the... Around 1945 or so, I think they finally got together.
Well, maybe it wasn't that long ago. Might have been...

Yeah. But they'd gone together... Anyway, say, 10 years or so ago, quite a while back. Anyway, George Barquet's brother, Sheil, who wasn't as well-known as George, down here at least, had passed for white for years. I know Mineta says he met him once on Canal Street after he started passing, and he said, well, I like it better. I forget. I have that in some of the Mineta interviews. Some of that stuff I'll copy, too, later on, which is on tape. He likes it better. Mineta sort of, you know, he wasn't mad at him or anything. Sometimes they are offended if they... Like Bunk would be. Bunk... There was one story there... Not a story. I mean, the fact that... When Bunk was in San Francisco... He was declaring that it's with Ellington for years. Barney Bigard. He wasn't trying to pass, but he just wanted to join the... He's light enough to pass, too. His brother is a little darker here, Alec Bigard. Barney wasn't trying to pass or give up the family or deny the family and all, like some people like Bill Johnson, we mentioned. But he did want to join the white local at that time, which was separate in Los Angeles, because they could get good movie jobs. And in fact, Barney did get some movie jobs there, even when he was a member of the colored local. But it would have been easier with the white local. And there was quite a big article in Downbeat once, in which Barney did actually come out that when he was trying to join the white local, said he wasn't a Negro, that he was really French, and went through that line. And he just played with Ellington because Ellington had hired him and all that for years, for 13 years. So he was going to come to town. In fact, he did come to town in San Francisco with the white band. He worked with white bands Freddie Slack for a while. And somebody else, I forget the other band. So he was to play with Bunk Johnson. I remember my friend Bill Colburn asked Bunk, short him the story in Downbeat, is this true that Alec Bigard isn't a Negro? And Bunk, he was so mad, he said, read the article, he said, no, he's not a Negro, he's a goddamn nigger. And Bunk was so proud of his color, he was very black. And we'd say, I'd rather be as black as that stove than as white as that sink. I mean, he really was. Not that he was trying to sour grapes or anything, he was proud of his colors. He couldn't understand anybody that wanted to pass. But Minetta did, of course, Minetta's quite light. He could pass almost too at any time. Probably, probably, well, I've seen him walk in white places with, even with me, that nobody would, even the Roosevelt Hotel, the jazz club must, nobody would know he was colored. So, he said, made some remark to Scheel Bakke, well, I see you're on the other side of the fence or something of that kind. And Scheel said, yes, I like it better, I like it better that way. Meaning you get better jobs and all that. So, he evidently didn't want to talk to anybody, the same as Bill Johnson refused to talk to any contacts that I tried to make with him those last three or four years. But I'll go over those Bakke notes. There's nothing especially to tell. Here's a note about Trixie Fragonza. A note in the San Francisco, St. Louis newspaper told the death of Trixie Fragonza at the age of 78 in 1949 in Pasadena. They called her an old vaudeville trooper.
